column5: shade and rest in the day’s heat
column6: The commentary has Musa withdraw to shade after watering the women; Genesis places Abraham at his tent entrance under the oaks in the heat of the day, a parallel of shelter after exertion.
The commentary joins water at the well with Musa’s retreat to shade; Abraham offers water to wash his visitors’ feet and rest under a tree, bringing water and shade together in hospitality.
The commentary follows water into food and livelihood; Abraham’s visitors are offered bread after water and rest, extending the same hospitality sequence from drink to food.

The commentary describes the mouth of a well and its beam, pulley, and bucket; Jacob’s scene identifies a large stone laid over the well’s mouth, giving a distinct biblical mechanism for controlling access to well water.

The commentary says the women wait to water until shepherds depart; Genesis has shepherds wait until all flocks gather before moving the stone and watering them, making control of access to a well part of the scene.

column5: Jacob opens the well and waters a flock
column6: The commentary’s Musa waters women’s flocks at a well; Jacob moves the stone from the well’s mouth and waters Rachel’s flock, another well-side meeting involving a woman and animal water.
The commentary links the road with the traveler’s need for water; Exodus says Israel travels through the wilderness and has no water to drink, making thirst an immediate danger of the route.
The commentary treats water as what keeps a traveler’s affairs standing; in the wilderness God brings water from the rock at Horeb for the people to drink.

column5: water gushes from the rock again
column6: The commentary presents water as life-sustaining provision; in a second wilderness account Moses strikes the rock and water gushes out for the congregation and their animals.
The commentary joins journey, well, and water for people and flocks; at Beer God tells Moses to gather the people and promises to give them water.
The commentary carefully develops the well’s mouth and the apparatus for drawing water; Israel sings to the well, “Spring up,” making a well itself the focus of a public water song.
The commentary says water is the support and “king” of communal affairs; Numbers says princes and nobles dug this well with their staffs, tying water access to leaders’ work.

column5: water from the deep in the wilderness
column6: The commentary explains that water holds up the traveler’s affairs; Psalm 78 recalls God splitting rocks in the wilderness and giving drink as from the deep.
The commentary moves between the deep well and water that sustains life; Psalm 78 says streams came from the rock and ran like rivers.

column5: water and food on the journey
column6: The commentary traces water toward food and livelihood; Psalm 78 recalls water gushing from the rock and immediately asks whether God can also provide bread and meat.
The commentary describes tender growth that survives summer and rain that revives the earth; Job says a felled tree still has hope of sprouting again.

column5: scent of water renews the tree
column6: The commentary says rain marks soil with green growth; Job’s tree buds and puts forth branches at the scent of water, making renewed vegetation a sign of life after apparent death.

column5: tree renewal beside the question of human life
column6: The commentary connects revived earth with the raising of the dead; Job asks whether a human who dies will live again after describing a tree renewed by water.
The commentary cites rain as a sign of the earth’s revival and connects rain to raising the dead; Hosea promises that God will revive Israel and raise it up on the third day.
The commentary’s rain revives dead earth and points toward resurrection; Ezekiel is told to promise breath to dry bones so that they will live.
The commentary links rain, renewed earth, and raising the dead; Ezekiel’s breath enters the bones, they live, and stand on their feet as a vast assembly.

column5: blessing or curse set before the people
column6: The commentary distinguishes those granted favor from those under wrath or astray; Deuteronomy explicitly sets blessing and curse before Israel in the same chapter that ties rain to obedience and harvest.
The commentary asks for the path of those given favor; Deuteronomy says blessing follows listening to the LORD’s commandments.
The commentary asks not to follow the straying path; Deuteronomy names a curse for disobeying and turning aside to other gods.

column5: life and good set against death and evil
column6: The commentary asks for the straight path and distinguishes its people from those who stray; Moses places life and good before Israel alongside death and evil.
The commentary seeks the way of those granted favor, not the way of wrath; Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses and sets life and death, blessing and curse before the people.

column5: hold fast to God, who is life
column6: The commentary asks to be guided on a path that sustains life; Deuteronomy says to love the LORD, listen to his voice, and hold fast to him because he is the people’s life.
The commentary’s central request is guidance on the straight path; Proverbs says that acknowledging God in all one’s ways results in God making the paths straight.
The commentary pairs the straight path with travel and water in the wilderness; Isaiah calls for a highway to be made straight in the desert for God.
The commentary asks for the straight path; Matthew applies Isaiah’s wilderness voice to John, who prepares the Lord’s way and makes his paths straight.
The commentary asks for guidance on a straight path; Mark opens John’s wilderness preaching with Isaiah’s call to prepare the Lord’s way.
The commentary’s sirat is a road to be made straight; Luke quotes Isaiah’s command to prepare the Lord’s way and make his paths straight.
The commentary asks to be guided on the straight path; John the Baptist identifies himself with Isaiah’s voice calling for the Lord’s way to be made straight.

column5: wind shelter, dry-land stream, and shade
column6: The commentary brings wind, water, and Musa’s shade together; Isaiah describes a refuge from wind and storm, streams in dry land, and shade from a great rock in a weary land.
The commentary says rain restores soil and makes it fruitful; Psalm 107 says God turns wilderness into a pool and parched land into springs.
The commentary moves from water to livelihood; Psalm 107 says God settles hungry people there and they establish a city to live in.
The commentary follows rain into plants and food; Psalm 107 describes sowing fields, planting vineyards, and obtaining a fruitful yield.
The commentary says rain improves people’s condition and feeds animals; Psalm 107 says God blesses the people so they multiply and their livestock increase.
The commentary calls God mālik on the Day of Judgment and says water is “our king”; Psalm 72 asks that the king judge the people with righteousness and the poor with justice.

column5: rain on cut grass under the king
column6: The commentary joins the kingly water image to rain-fed growth; Psalm 72 compares the king’s reign to rain falling on mown grass and showers watering the earth.

column5: grace and blessing for the people
column6: The commentary connects hamd with rain and mercy; Psalm 67 asks God to be gracious and bless the people before describing the earth’s yield and the nations’ praise.
The commentary traces rain to plants and food; Psalm 67 says the earth has yielded its increase and asks God to bless the people.
The commentary names the Lord of all worlds and invokes praise; Psalm 67 ends with all the ends of the earth fearing God after the earth’s harvest.
The commentary names God as ruler of the Day of Judgment and Lord of the worlds; Psalm 96 says the LORD reigns and judges the peoples with equity.

column5: God comes to judge the earth
column6: The commentary calls God the Owner of the Day of Judgment; Psalm 96 says God comes to judge the earth with righteousness and the peoples with faithfulness.
The commentary names the Day of Judgment; Daniel sees the court sit and books open, giving an apocalyptic court scene for divine judgment.

column5: a human-like figure approaches the Ancient of Days
column6: The commentary calls God the sovereign of the judgment day; Daniel sees one like a son of man come before the Ancient of Days in the heavenly court.
The commentary calls God mālik and Lord of all worlds; Daniel’s human-like figure receives dominion and a kingdom served by all peoples and nations.

column5: a fixed day to judge the world
column6: The commentary names the Day of Judgment; Paul says God appointed a day to judge the inhabited world in righteousness and gave assurance by raising the appointed man.

column5: feet guided into the way of peace
column6: The commentary asks God to guide “us” on a straight path; Zechariah’s hymn says the dawn from on high will guide people’s feet into the way of peace.

column5: a king longs for well water
column6: The commentary says a tribe calls its waters “our kings” because water holds affairs together; David, himself king, longs for a drink from the well of Bethlehem.

column5: men risk their lives to draw water
column6: The commentary says the traveler’s water lets him hold his affairs in hand; David’s men break through enemy lines to draw the well water he longs for.
The commentary treats water as the support of life and rule; David refuses to drink the water because it represents the blood of men who risked their lives to fetch it.
The commentary places rain, harvest, and the Day of Judgment together; the Mishnah says the world is judged at Sukkot concerning water, joining seasonal rain to a global judgment calendar.

column5: water drawing as a temple rite
column6: The commentary describes water drawn from a well and rain as divine provision; the Mishnah describes drawing water from Siloam for the Temple’s water libation, making water-drawing a liturgical act.

The commentary labels bism with S-M-W and develops Arabic sama for cloud, rain, and plant; Genesis uses the related Hebrew shamayim for the heavens, retaining the sky sense while the commentary’s Arabic examples extend it to what falls and grows.

The commentary distinguishes the path of those favored from the paths of wrath and straying; the Community Rule contrasts the spirits of truth and perversity and their opposed ways, giving a Jewish sectarian account of moral paths.

column5: way of light and way of darkness
column6: The commentary asks for the straight path rather than the paths of wrath and straying; Barnabas sets out a way of light against a way of darkness, a Christian ethical expansion of the two-way contrast.
The commentary connects rain-soaked soil, plant growth, and the raising of the dead; Paul says the seed is not made alive unless it dies, using planted growth to explain resurrection.

column5: a bare kernel becomes a plant
column6: The commentary says rain leaves a green trace on earth; Paul distinguishes the bare kernel sown from the body that will grow, making plant emergence a model for resurrection.
The commentary links renewed earth to the resurrection of the dead; Paul explicitly compares a perishable seed sown in the ground with the imperishable body raised.

The commentary says the first rain marks soil with green growth and distinguishes favored from rejected paths; Ezekiel orders a mark on the foreheads of those who grieve, so they are distinguished when judgment falls.
The commentary develops rain as a mark on the earth and distinguishes people on the final path; Revelation seals God’s servants before harm comes to earth, sea, and trees.
